hook: East and West separate over authority and the Creed; in 1965 pope and patriarch lifted the old excommunications

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nicaea II and veneration: the honor given an image passes to the one it shows. Your line was honor passes through.

"That there be no schisms among you." Saint Paul wrote that to a church in Corinth that was splitting into camps: I am of Paul, I am of Apollo. A schism is a tear. Not a disagreement, which a family can live with, but a tear in the fabric, where people who belong at one table stop sitting at it together. Paul begged that church not to tear. Long after, a tear came between two churches, East and West. Today, the year that stands for it, and the word for what happened: schism.
screen: `NO SCHISMS AMONG YOU.` → `A TEAR, NOT A DISAGREEMENT.` → `TWO CHURCHES, ONE TABLE.`

segments.voice: Two questions had been pulling the Latin West and the Greek East apart. The first was authority: the bishop of Rome's role among all the bishops. Catholics hold that the pope, as Peter's successor, has a primacy over the whole Church. Orthodox Christians honor Rome's place among the ancient churches but understand that primacy differently. The second was the Creed. In the West, the line about the Spirit came to read who proceeds from the Father and the Son. The Catechism says plainly that and the Son was not in the creed confessed at Constantinople, and that the Eastern tradition stresses the Father as the first origin of the Spirit, while the Latin tradition stresses the communion of Father and Son. Then came the moment the year stands for. The common declaration Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras made in 1965 recalls it: in 1054, legates of the Roman see pronounced a sentence of excommunication against the Patriarch of Constantinople, Michael Cerularius, and the patriarch and his synod answered with one of their own. In time it hardened into a lasting break. In that same declaration, the pope and the patriarch said they regretted the offensive words and gestures on both sides, and they removed the old excommunications from the memory and the midst of the Church. That didn't end the schism; the two churches are still not in full communion. But the curses are gone, and the two churches keep talking. A wound, still healing. And under all of it, Jesus's own prayer in John: "That they all may be one."
screen: `AUTHORITY: THE POPE'S ROLE.` · `THE CREED: AND THE SON.` · `A SENTENCE, AND AN ANSWER.` · then, large: `THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.` · then: `THE OLD CURSES, REMOVED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind an Orthodox church you've passed, a Greek or Russian or Romanian or Ukrainian neighbor, or the Orthodox Christians of the world at prayer today, who say the creed of Nicaea and Constantinople and venerate the icons Nicaea defended. If you pray, pray for them and for the day both churches share one table; if you don't, just wish them well, and stay with that wish.
Schism. A tear in the Church's unity, where people who belong at one table stop sharing it. Today's word.
Your line: a wound, still healing. Healing this slow is still healing, and it isn't finished yet. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity each January, and popes and ecumenical patriarchs have met, prayed together and signed common declarations since the excommunications were lifted.

chat.says: What actually happened in 1054 between Rome and Constantinople?
options: Rome's legates and the patriarch excommunicated each other; it hardened into a break.
A council voted to split the Church in two, and both sides signed it.
The pope closed every Orthodox church, and the break began that very day.
chat.meaning: In 1054 Rome's legates and Patriarch Michael Cerularius exchanged excommunications; in 1965 Paul VI and Athenagoras removed them, though full communion isn't yet restored.

primacy.meaning: first place; here, the bishop of Rome's role among the bishops

sources.ref: Joint Catholic-Orthodox Declaration of Pope Paul VI and Ecumenical Patriarch Athenagoras I (7 December 1965)

notes: The 1965 Joint Declaration recalls the 1054 sentence of excommunication against Patriarch Michael Cerularius and two others by Roman legates led by Cardinal Humbert, and the similar sentence by the patriarch and synod; it regrets offensive words and reprehensible gestures on both sides and removes the excommunications 'from memory and from the midst of the Church'. Paraphrased; the year 1054 in voice rests on this text. Confirm.
Primacy: Catholic view per CCC 882; Orthodox view summarized as honoring Rome's place among the ancient churches but understanding primacy differently. Confirm fairness; neither ranked.
CCC 247–248 on the Filioque paraphrased; confirm.

'They have been talking ever since' and howItsDone's meetings of popes and patriarchs: confirm.
